steps.why: The atlas edge: an offline score covers a fixed task distribution, but production traffic shifts. Monitoring carries the eval into deployment.

steps.objective: Design the escalation path: which cases go to a human reviewer, what the reviewer sees, and how to measure accuracy and cost of the agent plus reviewer against either alone.
steps.why: The atlas edge: monitors exist to trigger intervention. In a product, intervention usually means handing the case, or the whole workflow, to a person.

steps.objective: State the off-switch game's result (an agent uncertain about its objective, treating the human's choice as evidence, can prefer to stay interruptible) and the assumptions it needs (a rational human, a correct model).
steps.why: The atlas edge: the off-switch game explains, in a formal model, why an agent would defer to a human, while learned deferral rules add an empirical model of the human's errors. Escalation in the harness is the engineering form of being correctable.

steps.objective: State what the thesis asks of a correction interface and how its falsifier would show up in a deployed agent: better proxy scores alongside worse, independently measured user outcomes.
steps.why: Untested link: the off-switch result supplies the incentive part of the thesis's correction interface, under strong assumptions. The thesis asks for the evidence a harness can actually collect: corrections that hold up and user outcomes measured independently of the agent's own metrics.

paths.title: Inside the agent harness: schema-checked tool calls, end-state evals, abstention and escalation
paths.summary: Engineer an LLM agent that a customer can trust with real actions: tool calls checked against the API contract, schema-constrained outputs, end-state evals and model judges, sampling-based hallucination detection, abstention and escalation to people, and runtime monitoring that tells you when live risk has gone up.
paths.audience: Software engineers who ship LLM agents into customers' products (finance, legal, health, security, robotics, accessibility) and need them to be reliable, not just impressive in a demo. Assumes you have used an LLM API; no statistics background assumed.

steps.objective: Write a tool definition (name, description, JSON parameter schema), trace one call through the loop (model emits a call, your code executes it, the result goes back into context), and list three ways a well-formed call can still be wrong: wrong tool, wrong argument value, and an unauthorized side effect.
steps.why: Agents act through tools, so the API contract, not the model, is what defines an action. Start with the interface every later step checks, measures or blocks.

steps.objective: Explain how a JSON Schema or grammar is compiled to an automaton whose states mask invalid tokens at each decoding step, and state exactly what that guarantees (the output parses) and what it does not (the field values are right).
steps.why: The atlas edge: grammar or JSON-Schema masking guarantees that a tool call parses against the API contract, while choosing the right call stays the model's job. This removes one whole failure class, malformed calls, and isolates the rest.

steps.objective: Score an agent on end states (the database or repository after the episode) rather than on its transcript, compute pass^k (the chance that all k independent trials succeed) from repeated runs, and explain why pass^8 can sit far below single-trial success.
steps.why: There is no direct atlas edge from constrained decoding to evals. A call that parses can still be the wrong call, so the next question is whether the task actually got done, every time: measure end states over repeated trials instead of one lucky run.

steps.objective: Before splitting a task across planner, worker and critic agents, run the single-agent and self-consistency baselines at matched token budgets, and sort failed multi-agent traces into MAST's three categories: system design, inter-agent misalignment and task verification.
steps.why: The atlas edge: multi-agent LLM systems often gain little on popular benchmarks, so end-state checks and matched-compute single-agent baselines are needed before adding agents. Customers often ask for "a team of agents"; this is how you test whether it helps.

steps.objective: Build an LLM-judge rubric for outcomes that cannot be checked by code, test it for position bias (swap answer order), verbosity bias (pad one answer) and self-enhancement bias, and measure its agreement with expert labels on a stratified sample before it replaces human review.
steps.why: The atlas edge: MAST scales failure annotation with an LLM judge only after checking its agreement with expert annotations. You will need judges for most customer tasks, so learn to measure the judge before trusting it.

steps.objective: Sample several answers to one question, cluster them by bidirectional entailment, compute the entropy over the meaning clusters, and explain why a model that is consistently wrong can still have low semantic entropy.
steps.why: There is no direct atlas edge from judges to this step. Judges grade answers after the fact; semantic entropy flags likely confabulations at run time, before anyone sees them, using the same repeated sampling as pass^k.

steps.objective: Turn an uncertainty score into an answer-or-abstain rule, draw the risk–coverage curve, and pick the threshold that meets an error-rate target at the highest coverage; state Chow's rule for when abstaining is optimal given an abstention cost.
steps.why: The atlas edge: refusing the questions with the highest semantic entropy raises accuracy on those answered, a risk–coverage trade-off. A detector only helps once it drives a decision, and abstaining is the simplest decision.

steps.objective: Design an escalation rule that sends a case to a human reviewer when the reviewer is likely to do better than the model, and evaluate team accuracy and cost against model-only and human-only baselines at a fixed review budget.
steps.why: The atlas edge: learning to defer generalizes rejection by modelling the expert; it learns where the human is better instead of rejecting by model confidence alone. In customer deployments, an abstention usually means a handoff to a person.

steps.objective: Put an input–output policy classifier in front of and behind the agent, and set up a sequential test on live traffic that raises an alarm when the risk of harmful outputs rises, while controlling false alarms under benign drift; list the classifier's cost in refusals and compute.
steps.why: The atlas edge: sequential risk monitors exist to trigger intervention, such as expert review or retraining, when a harmful shift is detected. This closes the loop: everything measured offline in steps 3–8 is now watched in production.

paths.title: Shipping agents into regulated verticals: trading controls, model risk, the AI Act, legal, clinical and accessibility
paths.summary: Tour the regulated and high-consequence domains agents are deployed into, through one lens: what does a wrong or unintended action cost here, and which rule or control catches it. Finance (automated trading controls, model risk management), the EU AI Act, legal research, clinical decision support and accessibility.
paths.audience: Forward-deployed engineers about to put an LLM agent into a finance, legal, healthcare or accessibility customer, who know the engineering but not the domain's failure history or rules. Pairs with part I; no legal or clinical training assumed.

steps.objective: Retell the Knight Capital incident from the SEC order (an automated router, 45 minutes, over $460 million lost) and list the controls that were missing: hard pre-trade limits enforced outside the system, an automatic kill switch, and a release procedure that catches a partial deployment.
steps.why: Start where an automated actor in a customer's system lost the most money fastest. No learned model was involved, so the lesson is purely about the controls a harness puts around any automated actor: hard limits outside it, a kill switch and a careful release.

steps.objective: Describe what US bank model-risk guidance asks of a model (inventory, validation of conceptual soundness and outcomes, ongoing monitoring, effective challenge by independent experts) and note that the current guidance places generative and agentic AI outside its scope.
steps.why: The atlas edge separates two regimes: model-risk guidance covers quantitative models, market-access rules cover order flow, and Knight's loss came from deployment and missing controls. A finance customer will expect you to know which regime your agent falls under.

steps.objective: Explain how the EU AI Act tiers obligations by risk, name the duties on high-risk systems (risk management, logging, human oversight, robustness), and map NIST AI RMF's Govern, Map, Measure, Manage onto your own deployment pipeline.
steps.why: The atlas edge: because bank guidance defers generative and agentic AI to broader governance, the general AI frameworks are where an agent's obligations actually come from.

steps.objective: Explain why courts sanctioned a filing that cited non-existent cases, distinguish a fabricated citation from a real citation that does not support the stated claim (misgrounding), and design a check that resolves every citation against an authoritative database.
steps.why: The atlas edge: the AI Act lists AI that assists judicial authorities in researching and applying the law as high-risk. Legal work is where hallucinated authority has already caused sanctions, and retrieval reduced but did not remove it.

steps.objective: State when clinical decision support software stays outside FDA device regulation (the clinician must be able to independently review the basis of the recommendation), and explain why exam-style benchmark accuracy is not evidence of safe clinical use.
steps.why: There is no direct atlas edge from legal research; both are high-risk under the AI Act (step 3), legal by use case and medical AI through medical-device law. Health adds a second rule that shapes the product: a clinician must be able to check the basis of every recommendation.

steps.objective: Design the human-review step for a clinical assistant: what the reviewer sees, when cases are escalated, and how to measure team accuracy when the reviewer pool, workload or automation bias changes.
steps.why: The atlas edge: non-device clinical decision support must let the professional independently review the basis of a recommendation, which writes human review into the regulatory boundary. The escalation design is therefore part of compliance, not an optional extra.

steps.objective: Explain why abstention is the special case of deferral where the human is not modelled, and choose an abstention threshold from a risk–coverage curve under different costs for a wrong answer and for declining.
steps.why: The atlas edge: deferral generalizes rejection. When no reviewer is available, as for a user on their own, the remaining option is for the system itself to say it cannot tell.

steps.objective: Explain why a blind or low-vision user cannot check a confidently wrong scene description, describe VizWiz's answerability task, and weight evaluation errors by consequence (medication, currency) rather than counting them equally.
steps.why: The atlas edge: VizWiz poses predicting whether a question is answerable from the image as its own task, which is abstention for users who cannot verify. Accessibility is where the cost asymmetry between a wrong answer and "I can't tell" is sharpest.

paths.title: The math under the harness: proper scores, conformal guarantees, drift monitoring and safety filters
paths.summary: The cross-field ideas reliable agents borrow: proper scoring rules and calibration, conformal guarantees, online calibration and sequential monitoring for drift, safety filters from control theory (constraint shields and control barrier functions), and reward hacking as the general reason optimized agents game their checks.
paths.audience: Forward-deployed engineers who have shipped agents (part I) and want the statistics and control ideas underneath confidence thresholds, guardrails and action limits, explained from the ground up for someone without an estimation, control or statistics degree.

steps.objective: Compute the log score and Brier score for a set of probabilistic predictions, explain what makes a scoring rule (strictly) proper, and show why a proper score rewards reporting your true belief rather than hedging or exaggerating.
steps.why: Every threshold in the harness, whether to answer, escalate or block, reads a confidence score. Proper scoring rules are how you check that those scores mean what they say, so they come first.

steps.objective: Run split conformal prediction: compute nonconformity scores on a held-out calibration set, take the ⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉-th smallest as the threshold, and state the guarantee (marginal coverage at least 1−α under exchangeability) and what it does not promise (coverage for each subgroup or input).
steps.why: The atlas edge: measure coverage and proper score separately, since neither alone certifies useful decisions. Conformal prediction adds what a proper score lacks, a finite-sample guarantee that holds whatever model produced the scores.

steps.objective: Implement adaptive conformal inference, which raises or lowers the threshold after each observed miss or hit, and explain why it trades the finite-sample guarantee for long-run error control when the data distribution drifts.
steps.why: The atlas edge: adaptive conformal procedures extend prediction-set evaluation to online distribution change. Customer traffic is not exchangeable over months, so a one-time calibration goes stale.

steps.objective: Set up a sequential test that monitors a live error rate and alarms only on a harmful rise, with false alarms controlled at every time step at once (a time-uniform confidence sequence); sketch the alternative of tracking quality metrics with a state-space (Kalman) model and alarming on inconsistent innovations.
steps.why: The atlas edge: both replace a fixed calibration with sequential control as deployment data arrive. Monitoring is change detection: deciding, from a noisy stream, when the system you shipped has stopped being the system you validated.

steps.objective: Describe a predictive safety filter: it checks a proposed action against a model and confidence bounds, minimally modifies it if needed, and falls back to a previously certified plan; contrast its guarantee with that of a learned input–output classifier.
steps.why: The atlas edge: shields and predictive safety filters enforce stated constraints under model assumptions, while learned classifiers filter by policy without a formal guarantee. When an agent drives an actuator or moves money, you want the former.

steps.objective: Write the control barrier function condition ḣ(x, u) ≥ −α(h(x)) that keeps a system inside the safe set {x : h(x) ≥ 0}, and explain why enforcing it at every instant makes the safe set forward invariant (once inside, never leave).
steps.why: The atlas edge: CBF action filtering enforces a specified invariance inequality, not arbitrary semantic preferences. The barrier function is the most common concrete form of a safety filter.

steps.objective: Solve the CBF quadratic program min ‖u − u_ref‖² subject to the barrier constraint in closed form as a projection onto a half-space, apply it to an action proposed by a language or VLA planner, and say what the filter cannot protect (the semantic intent of the instruction).
steps.why: The atlas edge is exact: for control-affine dynamics with a single constraint and no input bounds, the CBF-QP safety filter is a Euclidean projection. This is the cleanest pattern for letting a model propose and a verified layer dispose.

steps.objective: Give a concrete example where optimizing a proxy reward lowers true return, and explain why a filter or test that only checks what was written down cannot prevent an optimizer from satisfying the letter of the objective rather than its intent.
steps.why: There is no direct atlas edge from safety filters to reward hacking. The filter in step 7 guarantees only what was specified; reward hacking is the general failure when the specification itself is a proxy.

steps.objective: Recognize specification gaming in a coding or research agent (editing tests, patching a grader, faking a timer), and design an eval that resists it: hidden scorers, tamper canaries in tests and graders, and review of every diff that touches evaluation code.
steps.why: The atlas edge: patching a grader raises the measured score while the intended task goes undone, a deployed instance of proxy optimization. This brings the theory back to the agents and evals you build in part I.

paths.title: From LLM inference and performance engineering to the alignment thesis: compute, compression and inference-time control
paths.summary: Start where serving engineers live (the roofline, quantization and the KV cache) and follow the state that decoding carries: a growing exact cache, a fixed-size recurrent state, and the predictive state that theory says is sufficient. Then spend test-time compute against verifiers, see how selection overoptimizes them, and end at inference-time interventions as candidate correction actuators for the alignment thesis. The last three links into theory and the thesis are untested hypotheses.
paths.audience: ML/LLM inference and performance engineers (kernels, serving, quantization, decoding) who think in FLOPs, bytes and latency, are comfortable with probability at the level of sampling and KL divergence, and want to see where their tools meet the atlas's alignment thesis. No control theory or learning theory is assumed; open the computational-mechanics topic first if predictive states are new.

steps.objective: Compute the arithmetic intensity of batch-1 decode and of prefill for a given model and GPU, place both on the roofline, and say which ceiling binds and why batching or fewer bytes per weight help.
steps.why: Home ground and the lens for the whole path: every later step either moves bytes, spends idle compute or decides what state to keep. Decode is memory-bound because each token rereads every weight.

steps.objective: Explain how GPTQ and AWQ choose low-bit weights, why weight-only quantization speeds memory-bound decode, and which evaluations can hide capability-specific damage.
steps.why: The most familiar lever: fewer bytes per weight move decode toward the compute roof. Carry one caveat forward: a small average loss can hide damage on rare inputs, the kind of distinction the thesis cares about.

steps.objective: Compute KV-cache bytes per token, explain why the cache grows linearly with context and batch, and describe how paging and prefix sharing change allocation but not the state per token.
steps.why: Once weights are small, the cache becomes the memory bottleneck (KIVI quantizes it to 2 bits). Think of the KV cache as a belief state about the conversation: lossless relative to the model, but growing without bound.

steps.objective: Contrast per-token decode memory and time for a KV cache and a linear recurrent unit, and explain what a fixed-size state must give up.
steps.why: A KV cache is a lossless but growing belief; a recurrent state is a fixed-size lossy one. Which distinctions survive the compression is exactly the thesis's semantic-sufficiency question.

steps.objective: State the definition of causal states (histories grouped by their predicted futures) and why they are the minimal sufficient statistic for prediction, then design a test of whether a trained recurrent state approximates them.
steps.why: Untested link: theory names the state worth keeping, the minimal one sufficient for predicting the future. It gives a target for “what should the cache or state retain?” that is not just perplexity.

steps.objective: Explain the compute-optimal allocation of test-time compute, when it beats a larger model at matched FLOPs, and when it does not.
steps.why: Untested link: extra inference compute can extract more usable information from what the state retains, but it cannot restore what was discarded. Here your FLOPs budget becomes a quality knob instead of a cost.

steps.objective: Describe best-of-n with a trained verifier, state the KL upper bound log n − (n−1)/n, and explain why gold reward falls at large n against a proxy.
steps.why: The simplest test-time strategy, and the cleanest Goodhart demonstration: selection alone, with no weight updates, overoptimizes an imperfect verifier. This is the thesis's falsifier in miniature.

steps.objective: Explain how inference-time intervention and controlled decoding change behaviour without weight updates, and list what they cost (latency, other capabilities) and what they do not change.
steps.why: From picking among samples to steering the computation itself: these are cheap, reversible actuators you can deploy like a serving feature. Their scorers and directions are proxies too.

steps.objective: State what the thesis requires of its correction interface (persistence, unrelated-capability retention, enforcement outside the model) and design a matched-cost comparison of prompt, inference-time intervention and fine-tuning corrections.
steps.why: Untested link: inference-time interventions count as correction actuators only if the effect persists and unrelated capability holds on independent evaluations, at a total cost the thesis's compute-and-usefulness gap accepts.

paths.title: Serving LLMs efficiently: memory-bound decoding, KV memory, batching and the inference budget
paths.summary: Follow one request through a serving stack: why attention and decoding are memory-bound, how IO-aware kernels, cache compression and paging manage KV memory, how continuous batching trades latency for throughput, and how lifetime inference cost changes both model sizing and test-time compute.
paths.audience: Engineers and researchers who want a systems view of LLM inference, or performance engineers who want each technique tied to its primary source and its limits. Assumes the transformer architecture.

steps.objective: Place prefill, decode and attention kernels on a roofline and identify which are memory-bound.
steps.why: The model that explains every optimization on this path.

steps.objective: Explain how tiling and online softmax keep attention exact while cutting HBM traffic, and why FLOPs stay quadratic.
steps.why: The classic case of a memory-bound kernel made faster without changing its output.

steps.objective: Describe attention sinks and heavy-hitter eviction, and explain why stable perplexity is not long-range recall.
steps.why: FlashAttention keeps attention exact; cache compression gives up exactness to bound memory at inference time.

steps.objective: Compute KV bytes per token and explain paging, block tables and copy-on-write prefix sharing.
steps.why: When the whole cache must be kept, the problem becomes allocating it without waste.

steps.objective: Explain iteration-level scheduling and selective batching, and how free KV memory limits batch size.
steps.why: Efficient KV memory lets more sequences share each weight read, which is what batching exploits.

steps.objective: Define energy and cost per accepted answer and explain why per-query figures do not transfer between deployments.
steps.why: Batching moves the throughput–latency frontier; the budget decides where on it to operate.

steps.objective: State the Chinchilla compute-optimal rule and how expected inference demand shifts the optimum toward smaller models trained longer.
steps.why: Lifetime inference cost feeds back into how large a model to train in the first place.

steps.objective: Compare a larger model with a smaller one plus test-time search at matched total FLOPs, and say when each wins.
steps.why: The other side of the same budget: compute can be spent per query instead of in pretraining.

paths.title: Smaller models and faster decoding: speculative decoding, distillation, MoE, pruning, quantization and LoRA
paths.summary: Start from speculative decoding's exact output guarantee, then work through the ways a model is made cheaper to run: distilled drafts and students, sparse experts, pruning, low-bit weights and low-rank adapters on quantized bases, with what each preserves and what it can lose.
paths.audience: Engineers and researchers who deploy or compress models and want the main compression and fast-decoding methods connected, with sources and caveats. Assumes basic probability (sampling, KL divergence).

steps.objective: State the acceptance rule and residual distribution, and explain why the output distribution equals the target model's.
steps.why: A speedup with an exact guarantee: the standard against which the lossy methods that follow are judged.

steps.objective: Write the temperature-softened distillation loss, explain the T² factor, and state what student–teacher agreement does and does not imply.
steps.why: Speculative speedups depend on how well the draft agrees with the target, and distillation is how drafts are aligned.

steps.objective: Explain top-1 routing, why FLOPs per token stay fixed as parameters grow, and what memory and communication costs remain.
steps.why: Switch Transformers were distilled into dense students; sparse experts are the opposite trade, more parameters at fixed FLOPs.

steps.objective: Distinguish unstructured and structured pruning, state the lottery-ticket hypothesis and its large-scale caveat, and explain expert pruning.
steps.why: Whole experts can be pruned after training; pruning is the general version of removing what the model does not need.

steps.objective: Explain outlier handling in LLM.int8, second-order rounding in GPTQ and salient-channel scaling in AWQ.
steps.why: Pruning and quantization combine in one pipeline (Deep Compression); quantization is the most widely deployed of the two.

steps.objective: Write the LoRA update, explain merging for zero added latency, and describe QLoRA and the learning–forgetting trade-off.
steps.why: A quantized base can still be adapted: QLoRA trains low-rank adapters on a frozen 4-bit model.
